report:
### Research Summary

Scientific evidence regarding whether a vegetarian diet directly increases life expectancy compared with eating meat is **mixed and nuanced**. 

Vegetarians generally exhibit lower overall mortality rates than the general population. However, when vegetarians are compared directly to **health-conscious meat-eaters** who share similar lifestyle habits—such as low smoking rates, regular physical activity, and higher socioeconomic status—the difference in overall life expectancy and all-cause mortality becomes small or statistically insignificant.

* **Cardiovascular Mortality:** Meta-analyses show that vegetarian diets consistently reduce the risk of mortality from ischemic heart disease, largely due to improved blood pressure, weight, and lipid profiles (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666667721000374).
* **Cohort Variances:** Studies yield differing results depending on the population examined. The North American Adventist Health Study 2 found a ~12% reduction in all-cause mortality among vegetarians compared to non-vegetarians (https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(24)00652-X/fulltext; https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1710093). Conversely, the British EPIC-Oxford study found no significant difference in all-cause mortality between vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002916523238332).

### Conclusion

A vegetarian diet is associated with lower cardiovascular mortality, but evidence does not conclusively demonstrate that eliminating meat increases overall life expectancy on its own. Much of the observed longevity benefit in vegetarians is strongly influenced by broader healthy lifestyle factors rather than the avoidance of meat alone.
